prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Checkout A/B Test Results (language en).
Grid: 7 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Metric" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Control" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Variant" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Lift" spans 1 col × 2 row; "p-value" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 263px
  col 2: header "Control › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 52px
  col 3: header "Control › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 113px
  col 4: header "Variant › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 49px · one-line width 50px
  col 5: header "Variant › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 110px
  col 6: header "Lift" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 7: header "p-value" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 55px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"The narrow metric column breaks “abandonment” inside the word and forces several labels into three or four lines. Some confidence intervals also wrap, making rows harder to scan."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"Confidence intervals stay on one line, but the very narrow metric column splits words such as “completion” and “abandonment” and makes the table unnecessarily tall."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Metric labels remain intact and the paired groups are balanced, but the currency and time confidence intervals wrap, splitting time values across lines."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"A generous metric column keeps most labels short, and corresponding control and variant columns align well. Currency and time intervals still wrap, with time values split across lines."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The metric labels have useful space, but both time means split over two lines, as do the time intervals, and the p-value header wraps."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"All means and confidence intervals stay intact on one line, while metric labels wrap naturally without breaking words. The control and variant groups have balanced widths and rows remain easy to compare."}},"best":["F"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"D gives the metric labels more room, so its wider first column could be preferred if label scanning matters more than keeping confidence intervals intact."}
